items.title: 52060_Eddie Barefield oral history interview
items.q: And then when Paul Mike Whiteman came up there as the president, he was conducting the Connie Boswell Show and I was in that orchestra, too.

ctx.x: Well, I remember definitely when we made the audition. And they had us to go up to the mike and play and sit down, play blending and all that. So now later on I was told by Sid Stoneberg that the whole reed section was on notice until I came in there. And when I came in they cancelled all the notices.

So I was over there on that staff for four years. And the conductors were like Joe Rines and Paul Levalle (PHONETIC) that did "Lower Basin Street" with Paul Levalle. Nathan Van Cleave (PHONETIC), Bernard Green, Joe Stokepack. And I did the Don McNeil's Breakfast Show whenever it came there, under the direction of Eddie Balentine. And then when Paul Mike Whiteman
came up there as the president, he was conducting the Connie Boswell Show and I was in that orchestra, too.

items.title: 52060_Eddie Barefield oral history interview
items.q: So it got even Paul Whiteman's band in the twenties, he had a big band but they never bothered with anything more than three part harmony.

ctx.x: And then eventually the thing became a standard style where they had two altos, two tenors and a baritone. And the trumpet started doing it. But it was an evolution. But everybody was still playing the same thing but it was just getting to be a more involved harmonic thing from playing

chords to utilizing the whole scale in your playing. And harmonization. Where before we played just three part harmony. Along about 1928 McKinney's Cotton Pickers came in adding the sixth. And this was an evolution. In fact, when I added the sixth to our chords out there in Minneapolis, the leader wouldn't play those arrangements because he said they sounded bad. And McKinney's Cotton Pickers started this and when Don Redman came in they started using five brass and six, you know, like that. So it got even Paul…
